nodes.statement: Let 0<T<infty, and dgeq 2. There exists an extension (tildeu_varepsilon,tildep_varepsilon) of the solution (u_varepsilon,p_varepsilon) to , which weakly converges in L^2(0,T;L^2(Omega)^d)times L^2(0,T;L^2(Omega)/R) to the unique solution (u_0,p_0) of the homogenized problem (known as Darcy's law with memory): left\ &u_0(x,t)=int_0^tds A(t-s)(f-nabla p_0)(x,s) &in& Omegatimes(0,T);\\ &nablacdot u_0=0 &in& Omegatimes(0,T);\\ &u_0cdot vecn=0 &on& partialOmegatimes (0,T), right. where vecn is the unit outward normal vector of partialOmega. The quantity A=(A_ij) is a symmetry, positive defined, and time-dependent permeability tensor, determined by A_ij(t)=int_Y_fdy W_j(y,t)cdot e_i, where e_i=(0,cdots,1,cdots,0) with 1 in the i^th place, and (W_j,pi_j)in L^2(0,T;H^1_per(Y_f)^d)times H^-1 (0,T;L^2_per(Y_f)/R) is the corrector associated with e_j by the following equations: left\ partial_t W_j-Delta W_j+ nabla pi_j&=0& &in omegatimes(0,T];\\ nablacdot W_j&=0& &in omegatimes(0,T];\\ W_j&=0& &on partialomega times(0,T],\\ W_j|_t=0&=e_j& &on omega. right. Moreover, there holds the strong convergence & int_0^Tdtbig\|tildeu_varepsilon(cdot,t) -int_0^tds W(cdot/varepsilon,t-s)(f-nabla p_0)(cdot,s)big\|_L^2(Omega)^2 to 0,qquadas varepsilonto 0.

nodes.statement: The fundamental reason for restricting the dimension to 2D or 3D in this paper is based on the technique of the corrector's estimate. As mentioned earlier, we are going to employ the interior Caccioppoli-type estimates, which utilizes the basic properties of the curl operator in three-dimensional case (see Lemma ). The high-dimensional generalization of these basic properties involves the redefinition of the curl operator. We do not intend to discuss this issue in the present work.

nodes.raw_latex:
\emph{In terms of the equation $\eqref{pde:B}$,
if $w_\varepsilon^{(2)}$ is regarded as an unknown vector field,
the problem ``$\nabla\cdot v =g$'' has no uniqueness of the solution  
(see e.g. \cite[Theorem III.3.1]{Galdi11}).
Thus, there is no contradiction with that the constructed vector field $-(\hat{\xi_{\varepsilon}}+\hat{\eta_{\varepsilon}})$ satisfies
the same equation $\eqref{pde:B}$ as $w_\varepsilon^{(2)}$ does.
In fact, the intractable problem is that we cannot simply grasp satisfactory  estimates from the equation $\eqref{pde:B}$. Instead, by the constructed object $(\xi_{\varepsilon},\eta_{\varepsilon})$, the problem has been reduced to studying each of them in $\eqref{pde:C}$, where 
the so-called Bogovskii's operator is involved (see e.g. \cite{Bogovskii79} 
or \cite[Section III.3]{Galdi11}).   
We finally mention that the methods of constructing solutions
for (1) and (2) in $\eqref{pde:C}$ are different (see Section $\ref{sec4}$).}

By definition, the flux corrector plays a crucial role in addressing the boundary layer effects. This feature is consistent with the flux corrector introduced in the context of elliptic homogenization problems.

\emph{The corrector $(W_j,\pi_j)$ defined in
\eqref{pde2.1} is taken from A. Mikeli\'c \cite{Mikelic94}, which slightly differs from
that given by G. Allarie \cite{Allaire92}, i.e.,
\begin{equation}\label{pde:1.3}
\left\{
\begin{aligned}
\partial_t w_j-\Delta w_{j}+\nabla
\tilde{\pi}_{j}&=e_j&\qquad&\text{in}\quad \omega\times(0,T];\\
\nabla\cdot w_j &=0&\qquad&\text{in}\quad
\omega\times(0,T];\\
w_j&=0&\qquad&\text{on}\quad\partial\omega\times(0,T];\\
w_j|_{t=0}&=0&\qquad&\text{in}\quad\omega,
\quad T>0.
\end{aligned}
\right.
\end{equation}
We observe that there holds the equality:
$\partial_t w_j(\cdot,t)=W_j(\cdot,t)$ for any $t\geq 0$,
in the sense of Stokes semigroup representation, up to a projection\footnote{
Let $\mathcal{A}:=P(-\Delta)$ and $P$ is the Helmholtz projection
(see e.g. \cite{Tsai18}). By functional analytic approach,
we have $w_j(\cdot,t)=\int_{0}^{t}ds\exp\{-(t-s)\mathcal{A}\}e_j$,
and then using a spectral
representation, one can derive $\partial_t w_j
= \exp\{-t\mathcal{A}\}e_j$. On the other hand, by noting that $P(\nabla\kappa) = 0$, there holds
$W_i(\cdot,t)=\exp\{-t\mathcal{A}\}e_i =
\exp\{-t\mathcal{A}\}P(e_i-\nabla \kappa)$.
Thus, combining the previous two formulas, the equality $\partial_t w_j = W_j$ holds
up to the projection $P$.}.
However, this relationship does not alleviate the complexity arising
from the incompatibility among the given data in the equations \eqref{pde2.1}
or \eqref{pde:1.3}. By modifying the initial conditions,
G. Sandrakov introduced a revised version of the corrector
equations \cite[Theorem 2]{Sandrakov97}. 
However, this modification did not resolve this incompatibility between the initial and boundary data.}

nodes.statement: It suffices to show the estimate for any tin(0,t_0), where t_0in (0,1/2) is usually a small number, while for the case t>t_0 it can be simply inferred from the semigroup estimate itself. Also, we merely establish the concrete proof in the case of d=3. For d=2, one can simply set tildeW_j(y_1,y_2,y_3,t) = (W_j(y_1,y_2),0,t); tildepi(y_1,y_2,y_3,t) =pi(y_1,y_2,t); tildeW_j(y_1,y_2,y_3,0) = e_j, j=1,2. It is not hard to verify that (tildeW_j,tildepi) satisfies the corrector equation in three dimensional case. Therefore, once three dimensional case is proved, two dimensional problem can be directly approached in this way. includegraphics[width=0.8textwidth]P8 captionsmall This figure provides a heuristic illustration of the decomposition of region Y_f in two dimensional case. Furthermore, it is important to note that region Y is a periodic domain. Firstly, we decompose the integral domain Y_f into two parts (see Figure ): (Y_f)_rho and Y_fsetminus(Y_f)_rho, where (Y_f)_rho:=\yin Y_f:dist(y,partial Y_s)geq 2rho\ for the parameter rho>0, which will be fixed later. In this respect, the desired estimate is reduced to showing: (For the ease of the statement, we omit the subscript of W_j in the proof.) bigg(int_Y_f|nabla W(cdot,t)|^2bigg)^1/2 lesssim bigg(int_Y_fsetminus(Y_f)_rho|nabla W(cdot,t)|^2bigg)^1/2 +bigg(int_(Y_f)_rho|nabla W(cdot,t)|^2bigg)^1/2=:I_1+I_2. The easier term is I_1, and by using H\"older's inequality and the semigroup estimates (see e.g. ) in the order, we obtain I_1lesssim rho^frac12-frac1p bigg(int_Y_f|nabla W(cdot,t)|^p bigg)^1/p lesssim rho^frac12-frac1p t^-frac12. We now turn to the second term I_2, and start from giving a family of cut-off functions, denoted by \chi_i\, which satisfy that chi_i(y):=chi_0(y+y_i), and (Y_f)_rhosubsetbigcup_iB(y_i,rho)subset (Y_f)_frac12rho. We assume that item chi_0in C_per^1(Y) is a cut-off function; item chi_0=1 on B(0,rho/2) and supp(chi_0)subset B(0,rho) with |nablachi_0|lesssim frac1rho; item For any point in the region (Y_f)_rho, it is covered by, at most, five elements of the covering family \B(y_i,rho)\. nodes.statement: In general, we adopt a similar strategy and notation as presented in Lemma , with the additional use of an interpolation argument. The entire proof is structured into four steps. Step 1. One step reduction. The main idea is that we firstly improve the decay estimate in L^2-spatial norm, and then appeal to the interpolation argument to get a weaker improvement in terms of L^r-spatial norms with rnot= 2. Thus, the key step is to establish the following estimate: (Here we omit the subscript of W_j throughout the proof.) bigg(int_Y_fdy|Delta W(y,t)|^2bigg)^1/2lesssim t^-gamma for any t>0. Admitting the above estimate for a while, we introduce the infinitesimal generator A:=P(-Delta), where the operator P is known as the Helmholtz projection, and then it follows from the boundedness of P and that \|AW(cdot,t)\|_L^2(Y_f)= \|P(-Delta)W(cdot,t)\|_L^2(Y_f)leq \|Delta W(cdot,t)\|_L^2(Y_f)lesssim t^-gamma. Recalling Stokes semigroup estimates (see e.g. ): for 1<q<infty, we have \|A W(cdot,t)\|_L^q(Y_f)lesssim t^-1. Then, by preferring a suitable qin(1,infty) such that q<rleq 2 or 2leq r<q, one can employ the interpolation inequality to get that \|AW(cdot,t)\|_L^r(Y_f)&leq \|AW(cdot,t)\|^lambda_L^2(Y_f) \|AW(cdot,t)\|^1-lambda_L^q(Y_f)\\ &lesssim t^-1+lambda(1-gamma), where lambda:=frac2(q-r)r(q-2). Using the representation of the solution of by the semigroup theory, we have partial_t W = A W in Y_ftimes (0,infty), which implies the stated estimate . Step 2. A further reduction. The remainder part of the proof is devoted to establishing the crucial estimate from two important ingredients. Introducing the parameter rho>0, we decompose the following integral into two parts: the inner part and the near-boundary part, i.e., bigg( int_Y_f|Delta W(cdot,t)|^2 bigg)^1/2leq bigg( int_(Y_f)_rho|Delta W(cdot,t)|^2 bigg)^1/2+ bigg( int_Y_fsetminus(Y_f)_rho|Delta W(cdot,t)|^2 bigg)^1/2. Let pgeq 2, and we claim that there hold bigg( int_(Y_f)_rho|nabla^2W(cdot,t)|^2 bigg)^1/2&lesssim rho^-3t^-fracp3p-2;\\ bigg( int_Y_fsetminus(Y_f)_rho|Delta W(cdot,t)|^2 bigg)^1/2 &lesssim rho^frac12-frac1pt^-1. Admitting the above two estimates temporarily, we can proceed with our analysis. Inserting and back into , we have bigg(int_Y_f|Delta W(cdot,t)|^2bigg)^1/2lesssim rho^-3t^frac-p3p-2+ rho^frac12-frac1pt^-1, and minimizing the right-side above by taking rho>0 such that rho^-3t^frac-p3p-2= rho^frac12-frac1pt^-1, there holds bigg(int_Y_f|Delta W(cdot,t)|^2bigg)^1/2lesssim t^frac-p(19p-14)(3p-2)(7p-2), which gives us the core estimate by setting gamma:=fracp(19p-14)(3p-2)(7p-2). The desired estimate is reduced to estimating the first term in the bracket above. We also note that the interior estimate is translation-invariant within Y_f, and thus the center position of the estimated region can be disregarded. Therefore, we only need to establish the following estimate: int_0^Tdt\|nabla^2 W(cdot,t)\|^2_L^2(B/2) &lesssim\|nabla^2chi\|^2_L^infty(Y) int_0^Tdt\|nabla W(cdot,t)\|^2_L^2(2B), where B:=B(y,2rho) with 2Bsubset omega is arbitrary, and chiin C^infty_per(Y) is a cut-off function satisfying chi = 1 in B and supp(chi)subset 2B with |nablachi|lesssim frac1rho. Then, we turn to study the estimate . Set v=curl~W in omegatimes[0,T]. By recalling the equations , there holds a new parabolic system: left\ (partial_t-Delta)v&=0& &in Y_ftimes(0,T];\\ v|_partial Y_f&=curl~ W& &for 0<tleq T;\\ v|_t=0&=0.& & right. For we are interested in the interior estimates, by setting u=chi v, from the above parabolic system we get left\ (partial_t-Delta)u&=-Delta chi v-2nablachicdotnabla v:=g& &in Y_ftimes(0,T];\\ u|_partial Y_s&=0,& &for 0<t<T;\\ u|_t=0&=chi v|_t=0=0.& &\\ right. Thus, from the interior H^2 estimates for elliptic equation (see e.g. ), it follows that \|nabla^2 W(cdot,t)\|_L^2(B/2) lesssim \|nabla chi\|_L^infty(Y)\|nabla W(cdot,t)\|_L^2(B)+ \|curl~ v(cdot,t)\|_L^2(B) holds for any t>0. Hence, integrating both sides above with respect to t from 0 to T, we can derive that int_0^Tdt\|nabla^2 W(cdot,t)\|^2_L^2(B/2) &lesssim \|nabla chi\|^2_L^infty(Y) int_0^Tdt\|nabla W(cdot,t)\|^2_L^2(B) +int_0^Tdt\|nabla v(cdot,t)\|^2_L^2(B)\\ &oversetlesssim \|nabla^2chi\|^2_L^infty(Y) bigg\int_0^Tdt\|nabla W(cdot,t)\|^2_L^2(B) +int_0^Tdt\|v(cdot,t)\|^2_L^2(2B)bigg\\\ &lesssim\|nabla^2chi\|^2_L^infty(Y) int_0^Tdt\|nabla W(cdot,t)\|^2_L^2(2B), which is the stated estimate . Step 4. Show the estimate . We start from rewriting the equations as follows: for any t>0, left\ -Delta W(cdot,t)+nabla pi(cdot,t)&=-partial_t W(cdot,t) & &in Y_f;\\ nablacdot W(cdot,t)&=0& &in Y_f;\\ W(cdot,t)|_partial Y_s&=0.& & right. For any 1<p<infty, from the L^p theory for stationary Stokes system (see e.g. ), it follows that \|nabla^2W(cdot,t)\|_L^p(Y_f) +\|nablapi(cdot,t)\|_L^p(Y_f) lesssim \|partial_tW(cdot,t)\|_L^p(Y_f), where the up to constant depends on p,d and the character of Y_f. Then, for any pgeq 2, by using H\"older's inequality, the estimate , and the observation partial_t W =AW, as well as, Stokes semigroup estimates (see e.g. ), in the order, we obtain that bigg( int_Y_fsetminus(Y_f)_rho|Delta W(cdot,t)|^2 bigg)^1/2 &lesssimrho^frac12-frac1p bigg( int_Y_fsetminus(Y_f)_rho|nabla^2 W(cdot,t)|^p bigg)^1/p\\ &lesssim rho^frac12-frac1p bigg( int_Y_f|partial_t W(cdot,t)|^p bigg)^1/p =rho^frac12-frac1p bigg( int_Y_f|A W(cdot,t)|^p bigg)^1/plesssim rho^frac12-frac1pt^-1, which is the desired estimate . We have completed the whole proof.

nodes.statement: The advantage of the present proof avoids using advanced analysis resultsfootnoteThe case alpha =1 simply come from a testing function argument, and we pursue a consistency even in this refined estimate, although there exists a way to save effort on the pressure term.. We firstly establish the weighted estimate for partial_t W_j, and then translate the same type estimate to the pressure term pi_j. To do so, we take partial_t W_j as the test function for the equations , and for any t>0 there holds: int_Y_f|partial_t W_j(cdot,t)|^2 + frac12fracddtint_Y_f|nabla W_j(cdot,t)|^2 = 0. Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to temporal variable from tau to T, and then appealing to Lemma , we obtain that int_tau^Tint_Y_f|partial_t W_j|^2 leq frac12int_Y_f|nabla W_j(cdot,tau)|^2 lesssim tau^-2vartheta. Multiplying the factor tau^alpha-1 on the both sides above, and then integrating with respect to tau from 0 to T, one can further derive that int_0^Tdtau bigg(tau^alpha-1int_tau^Tint_Y_f|partial_t W_j|^2bigg) lesssim T^alpha-2vartheta. By using Fubini's theorem in the left-hand side above, i.e., int_0^Tdtau bigg(tau^alpha-1int_tau^Tint_Y_f|partial_t W_j|^2bigg) = int_0^Tdtint_Y_f|partial_t W_j(cdot,t)|^2t^alpha, we have established the following estimate int_0^Tdtint_Y_f|partial_t W_j(cdot,t)|^2t^alpha lesssim T^alpha-2vartheta. We now continue to study the pressure term, and begin with constructing an auxiliary function associated with Bogovskii's operator, i.e., for any t>0, we have left\ nablacdot v(cdot,t)&=pi(cdot,t),& &in~Y_f;\\ v(cdot,t)&=0,& &on~partial Y_s, ymapsto v(y,t)~is 1-periodic right. with the estimate \|v(cdot,t)\|_H^1(Y_f) lesssim\|pi(cdot,t)\|_L^2(Y_f). By taking v as a test function acting on , it is not hard to get int_Y_f|pi_j(cdot,t)|^2lesssimint_Y_f|partial_t W_j(cdot,t)|^2. Consequently, multiplying t^alpha on the both sides above and then integrating it from 0 to T, we obtain int_0^Tdtint_Y_f|pi_j(cdot,t)|^2t^alpha lesssim int_0^Tdtint_Y_f|partial_t W_j(cdot,t)|^2t^alpha oversetlesssim T^alpha-2vartheta. This together with leads to the desired estimate , and ends the whole proof.

nodes.name: antisymmetry and regularities
nodes.statement: For any 0<t<T, let B(cdot,t)=\b_ij(cdot,t)\_1leq i,jleq d be given as in Propostion . Then there hold the structure properties: (i)~~nablacdot B(cdot,t)=0; (ii)~~int_YB(cdot,t)=0. Moreover, there exists Phi(cdot,t)=\Phi_ki,j(cdot,t)\_1leq i,j,kleq d with Phi_ki,j(cdot,t)in H^1_loc(R^d) being 1-periodic, and satisfying nabla cdot Phi(cdot, t) = B(cdot,t) in Y under the antisymmetry condition (i.e., Phi_ki,j=-Phi_ik,j). Also, for any 1<q<infty, we have the regularity estimate \|Phi(cdot,t)\|_W^1,q(Y)lesssim \|B(cdot,t)\|_L^q(Y), where the up to constant is independent of t.

nodes.statement: In the previous work , to estimate E_2^i(t), we mainly relied on the periodicity of the flux corrector. Therefore, we made a more detailed division for O_varepsilon. However, this method becomes very complicated when addressing the decomposition of the three-dimensional boundary layer. Another obvious drawback is that it can only indicate the existence of the required decomposition for specific regions in R^3. As given in the above proof, we now turn to make more in-depth use of the antisymmetry property of the flux corrector. This improvement greatly simplifies the decomposition process for boundary layers (see Remark ).

As the argument developed by J.-L. Lions , for a.e. t>0, we introduce a function hatp(cdot,t) as the solution of left\ nablacdotBig[A(0)nablahatp(cdot,t)-int_0^tds A'(t-s)nabla p(cdot,s) Big]&=0,& &in~Omega;\\ vecncdotBig[A(0)nablahatp(cdot,t)-int_0^tds A'(t-s)nabla p(cdot,s) Big]&=0,& &on~partialOmega,\\ int_Omegahatp(cdot,t)&=0. right. Denote the operator nablacdot A(0)nabla =|Y_f|Delta by L, and K_0(p)(cdot,t): = int_0^tdsA'(t-s)nabla p(cdot,s); K_1(p): = L^-1nablacdot K_0(p). Then, the solution hatp of can be represented by hatp(cdot,t) = K_1(p)(cdot,t) in Omega. By Schauder estimates (see e.g. ), there holds that \|hatp(cdot,t)\|_C^2,1/2(barOmega)&leq C_1 bigg\|int_0^tds A'(t-s)nabla p(cdot,s)bigg\|_C^1,1/2(barOmega)\\ &leq C_1 int_0^tds |A'(t-s)|\|nabla p(cdot,s)\|_C^1,1/2(barOmega) leq C_1int_0^tds |A'(t-s)|\| p(cdot,s)\|_C^2,1/2(barOmega), where C_1 depends on |Y_f|, d, and Omega. In view of , we observe that LK_1(p) = nablacdot K_0(p), and therefore the equations can be rewritten as left\ LBig[p_0(cdot,t)+K_1(p_0)(cdot,t)Big] &=nablacdotBig[ int_0^tdsA'(t-s)f(cdot,s)+A(0)f(cdot,t) Big]& &in~Omega;\\ fracpartialpartialnuBig[p_0(cdot,t)+K_1(p_0)(cdot,t)Big]&= vecncdotBig[ int_0^tdsA'(t-s)f(cdot,s)+A(0)f(cdot,t) Big]& &on~partialOmega, right. where the conormal derivative associated with L is defined by partial/partialnu:=vecncdot A(0)nabla. Similarly, its solution can be expressed by big(p_0+K_1(p_0)big)(cdot,t)=L^-1 nablacdotBig[ int_0^tdsA'(t-s)f(cdot,s)+A(0)f(cdot,t) Big]=:tildef_1(cdot,t). Thus, for some T_1>0 (which will be fixed later), if constructing the following map: T_1(p) := tildef_1 - K_1(p) forall pin L^q(0,T_1; C^m+1,alpha(barOmega)), the unique existence of the solution of in L^q(0,T_1; C^m+1,alpha(barOmega)) is reduced to verifying that the map T_1: L^q(0,T_1; C^m+1,alpha(barOmega))to L^q(0,T_1; C^m+1,alpha(barOmega)) is a strict contraction. To see this, appealing to Schauder estimates again, we firstly derive that \|tildef_1(cdot,t)\|_C^m+1,alpha(barOmega)lesssim int_0^tds|A'(t-s)|\|f(cdot,s)\|_C^m,alpha(barOmega) +|A(0)|\|f(cdot,t)\|_C^m,alpha(barOmega). By integrating both sides of and with respect to t from 0 to T_1, Young's inequality, we obtain \|K_1(p)\|_L^q(0,T_1;C^m+1,alpha(barOmega)) &lesssim \|A'\|_L^1(0,T_1) \|p\|_L^q(0,T_1;C^m+1,alpha(barOmega));\\ \|tildef_1\|_L^q(0,T_1;C^m+1,alpha(barOmega)) &lesssim \|A'\|_L^1(0,T_1) \|f\|_L^q(0,T_1;C^m,alpha(barOmega)) + \|f\|_L^q(0,T_1;C^m,alpha(barOmega)). Then, it follows from the estimates and that \|T_1(p)(cdot,t)\|_C^m+1,alpha(barOmega) &leq \|K_1(p)(cdot,t)\|_C^m+1,alpha(barOmega)+ \|tildef_1(cdot,t)\|_C^m+1,alpha(barOmega)\\ &lesssim int_0^tds|A'(t-s)| big(\|p(cdot,s)\|_C^m+1,alpha(barOmega) +\|f(cdot,s)\|_C^m,alpha(barOmega)big) + \|f(cdot,t)\|_C^m,alpha(barOmega), and this implies &\|T_1(p)\|_L^q(0,T_1;C^m+1,alpha(barOmega)) \\ & lesssim \|A'\|_L^1(0,T_1) big(\|p\|_L^q(0,T_1;C^m+1,alpha(barOmega)) +\|f\|_L^q(0,T_1;C^m,alpha(barOmega))big) + \|f\|_L^q(0,T_1;C^m,alpha(barOmega)). Also, it is not hard to see thatfootnoteBy the definition, the operator K_1 is linear. \|T_1(u)-T_1(v) \|_L^q(0,T_1;C^m+1,alpha(barOmega)) oversetlesssim \|A'\|_L^1(0,T_1) \|u-v\|_L^q(0,T_1;C^m+1,alpha(barOmega)). Thus, by Lemma we know that A'in L^1(0,T), and due to the absolute continuity of the integral, for any epsilon>0, there exists delta>0 such that for any interval Isubset (0,+infty) with |I|leq delta, we have int_I|A'|<epsilon. Hence, there exists delta_0>0 such that for T_1=delta_0, the estimate turns to be \|T_1(u)-T_1(v) \|_L^q(0,delta_0;C^m+1,alpha(barOmega)) leq frac12\|u-v\|_L^q(0,delta_0;C^m+1,alpha(barOmega)). This coupled with verifies the contraction property of T_1 in L^q(0,delta_0;C^m+1,alpha(barOmega)). Consequently, it follows from Banach's fixed-point theorem that there exists unique solution p_0 such that T_1(p_0) = p_0 in L^q(0,delta_0;C^m+1,alpha(barOmega)), and this together with the estimate leads to the desired result \|p_0\|_L^2(0,delta_0;C^2,1/2(barOmega))lesssim \|f\|_L^2(0,delta_0;C^1,1/2(barOmega)). We have completed the proof.
